what_its_for: Ethacrynic acid is a strong water pill (diuretic) that helps your body get rid of extra fluid and salt through your urine. It is used to treat swelling (edema) caused by heart failure, liver disease, or kidney disease. It may also be used when other water pills have not worked for you.
how_to_take: Take this medicine by mouth with food or milk to help prevent an upset stomach. Take it exactly as your doctor tells you. Try to take it early in the day (morning or early afternoon) so that needing to urinate does not keep you up at night. Swallow the tablet whole with a full glass of water.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose for you based on your condition. A typical starting dose for adults is 50 mg once daily, and your doctor may adjust it up or down depending on how your body responds. Do not change your dose on your own. Your doctor will use the lowest dose that controls your swelling.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — but only if it is still early in the day. If it is already late in the afternoon or evening, skip the missed dose and take your next dose at the regular time the following morning. Never take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store this medicine at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep it away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Dispose of any unused or expired medicine safely — ask your pharmacist how.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol, as it can increase dizziness and dehydration. Do not stand up too quickly from sitting or lying down, as this medicine can cause dizziness or lightheadedness. Avoid getting too little fluid — drink enough water unless your doctor tells you to limit fluids. Be careful with salt substitutes, as many contain potassium, and your doctor may need to monitor your potassium levels closely. Avoid prolonged exposure to the sun without protection, as this medicine may make your skin more sensitive to sunlight.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away if you notice: sudden or severe hearing loss, ringing in your ears, or dizziness (these are important warning signs); signs of dehydration such as extreme thirst, dry mouth, little or no urination, or feeling very weak; muscle cramps, weakness, or irregular heartbeat (may be signs of low potassium); severe stomach pain, nausea, or vomiting; unusual bleeding or bruising; or signs of an allergic reaction such as rash, itching, swelling of the face or throat, or trouble breathing.
when_it_works: You should start to urinate more and notice some reduction in swelling within 30 minutes to 1 hour after taking your first dose. Maximum effect usually happens within 2 hours. Over several days of regular use, you should see ongoing improvement in swelling and fluid build-up. Keep taking it even if you feel better, unless your doctor tells you to stop.
special_populations: Older adults: You may be more sensitive to the effects of this medicine, including dizziness and dehydration. Use with extra caution and report any side effects to your doctor right away. Pregnancy: This medicine is generally not recommended during pregnancy. Talk to your doctor about the risks and benefits. Breastfeeding: It is not known if this medicine passes into breast milk. Ask your doctor before breastfeeding. Children: This medicine can be used in children, but the dose will be carefully adjusted by the doctor based on the child's weight. People with hearing problems: This medicine carries a higher risk of hearing damage if you already have hearing difficulties or if you are also taking other medicines that affect hearing. Tell your doctor about any hearing issues before starting this medicine.
